summary: Highlights outstanding architectural issues about deploying and using QoS mechanisms in the Internet, and where further standards work may help. It is the outcome of a collaborative exercise.

eli5.summary: This lists the unsolved problems with giving some Internet traffic priority treatment.

questions: what is qos in the internet
how do integrated services and differentiated services differ
why is qos hard to deploy
how does tcp interact with qos
subtitle: Outstanding problems in deploying quality-of-service mechanisms.

tldr.problem: The Internet offers best-effort service to all traffic equally. Two main QoS architectures (Integrated Services and Differentiated Services) existed, but both had significant gaps that prevented coherent end-to-end service delivery.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB examined the state and limitations of state-based QoS (per-flow reservations) and stateless QoS (per-packet markings), identifying 12 major areas where further standards work was needed.
tldr.outcome: The report highlighted that neither architecture alone could solve QoS deployment: IntServ required per-flow state that did not scale to the Internet core; DiffServ was simple but lacked end-to-end signaling. Both needed integration and refinement.

today: RFC 2990 is an Informational report from the IAB highlighting the challenges of deploying QoS. DiffServ has been more widely deployed than IntServ, largely because of its simplicity and scalability, but the RFC's predicted issues have largely come to pass: heterogeneous deployment across domains, lack of end-to-end service discovery, no standard measurement mechanisms, and limited application integration. IntServ remains important in controlled environments such as enterprise networks and MPLS-enabled carrier backbones. The fundamental tension between state-based and stateless approaches, and the need for application awareness, remain unresolved.

sections.title: The QoS Challenge
sections.content:
The Internet was designed to offer best-effort service: every packet is treated equally, and the network makes no commitment about delivery time, loss rate, or bandwidth. As the Internet carried more real-time applications like voice and video, operators wanted to offer differentiated services with superior or predictable performance for certain applications.

Two main architectures emerged: Integrated Services (IntServ), in which applications signal their requirements to the network and the network reserves resources per flow; and Differentiated Services (DiffServ), in which packets are marked with a service code point, and routers treat marked packets with corresponding service profiles without maintaining per-flow state. Both architectures have merit, but both had significant gaps that the IAB identified and documented.
sections.eli5: Some programs, like video calls, need fast service. Two big ideas exist for giving them priority. Both have problems that need solving.

sections.title: State-Based and Stateless Models
sections.content:
Integrated Services uses state-based admission control. An application signals its traffic profile (rate and burst size) using RSVP (Resource Reservation Protocol). If the network has enough resources, all routers along the path install reservation state for that flow. The router then schedules packets from that flow with the promised service level. This allows precise, per-application guarantees but requires every router to maintain and update flow state, which consumes memory and CPU proportional to the number of active flows.

Differentiated Services uses stateless packet marking. Applications or ingress routers mark each packet with a service code point (a 6-bit field in the IP header). Interior routers apply a corresponding per-hop behavior without checking flow state or traffic contracts. This scales well (routers do not track individual flows) but is imprecise: the network cannot guarantee service to individual applications, only provide aggregate behavior per service class. If the network becomes overloaded, no entity informs the application that the requested service is not being delivered.
sections.eli5: Integrated Services: each app asks permission and routers remember it (hard to scale). Differentiated Services: apps mark packets and routers treat marked packets nicely (simple but unpredictable).

sections.title: Applications and Awareness
sections.content:
A fundamental tension exists: should applications be aware of QoS, or should QoS be transparent?

Integrated Services requires applications to know about QoS. An application must predict its traffic profile and signal RSVP, and it must be prepared to learn if the network denies the request. This requires API changes and application modifications. Differentiated Services does not explicitly require application awareness—a network operator can assign service policies without the application knowing—but then the application cannot adapt its behavior based on network feedback. If quality of service degrades, the application has no way to learn about it. High-quality service ultimately requires either over-provisioning (extra resources to absorb any traffic) or explicit application involvement, or both.
sections.eli5: If apps know about QoS, they can ask nicely and adapt if denied. If apps do not know, the network can try to help, but apps cannot learn when things go wrong.

sections.title: Routing, Discovery, and Resource Management
sections.content:
Current QoS architectures assume the best-effort routing path carries QoS traffic. If a network offers multiple service classes along different paths, how does an application discover which paths support which services? No existing mechanism in either architecture supports QoS-aware path discovery.

Furthermore, efficient use of network resources would require traffic engineering: the ability to load-balance traffic across multiple paths based on the quality attributes each path can provide. This requires dynamic calculation of path quality vectors (not just the path with lowest metric) and the ability to distribute traffic across multiple paths. Neither IntServ nor DiffServ currently address this at scale. QoS routing research exists in academia but has not been integrated into standards or widely deployed.
sections.eli5: QoS routing needs to find paths that have the right kind of service available. It also needs to spread traffic smartly across paths to avoid overloading any single link. This is not defined yet.

sections.title: TCP and Traffic Conditioning
sections.content:
TCP is a congestion-controlled protocol: it adjusts its transmission rate based on feedback from acknowledgment packets. If the forward data packets receive high-quality service but the reverse acknowledgment stream is treated poorly, TCP throughput suffers unpredictably. Additionally, traffic conditioners in QoS networks typically use token bucket shapers, which drop tail packets when a bucket is full. Tail drops cause TCP to interpret them as congestion signals and perform full retransmission timeouts, unduly penalizing throughput.

A better approach for TCP is weighted Random Early Detection (RED), which drops packets probabilistically before a queue fills, giving TCP more time to react. The RFC notes that this is an open research area: the interaction between TCP's congestion control and network QoS mechanisms involves complex control loops and time constants that must be carefully tuned.
sections.eli5: TCP depends on getting reply packets quickly. If the replies are delayed, TCP slows way down. Queueing mechanisms designed for QoS can be unfriendly to TCP if they drop tail packets.

sections.title: Measurement, Accounting, and Deployment Diversity
sections.content:
QoS architectures lack standard methods to measure whether delivered service matches the promised levels. Network operators need objective measurements to verify they are delivering the advertised service quality. Clients also need to measure delivered quality to justify premium service costs. Without measurement, neither party can resolve disputes.

If premium services attract surcharges, usage-based accounting becomes necessary, but neither architecture defines an accounting model. Additionally, no two networks are likely to deploy the same QoS architecture. Some will use IntServ, others DiffServ, others nothing. Service capability discovery becomes critical in this heterogeneous environment, but neither architecture includes clear discovery mechanisms. The RFC notes that this heterogeneity creates scaling pressure in routing, as each path to each destination becomes qualified by its service capabilities, multiplying the potential routing entries.
sections.eli5: How do you prove you delivered good service? Who pays if it is not good? And different networks will use different QoS systems, so apps must discover what each network offers.
